content:
Paul's claim to speak for Jesus rests on one event: the risen Jesus appeared to him on the road to Damascus. Christians are told that the event is recorded in Scripture, three times over. The three records do not agree.

Acts tells the story once as narrative, in chapter 9, and twice in speeches given to Paul, in chapters 22 and 26. The Catholic New American Bible says plainly that the accounts come "with some differences of detail owing to Luke's use of different sources."[1]

This article aims to provide context to the three accounts, insha'Allah, in five differences between them, each set beside the explanation Christians give. We set out what the event meant for Paul's standing in Paul's claim to apostleship.

In Acts 9, "the men who traveled with him stood speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one" (Acts 9:7). In Acts 22, Paul says: "Those who were with me indeed saw the light and were afraid, but they didn't understand the voice of him who spoke to me" (Acts 22:9).[2] The Greek word in both verses is phōnē, voice or sound. The King James Version translates both the same way: in chapter 9 they were "hearing a voice", and in chapter 22 "they heard not the voice".

The usual defence turns on grammar. The verb "hear" takes the genitive case in 9:7 and the accusative in 22:9, and the claim is that the first means hearing a sound and the second understanding words. Daniel Wallace, whose Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics is a standard text in evangelical seminaries, examined the claim and found that Luke does not keep that distinction elsewhere.[3]

Modern translations that render 22:9 as "didn't understand" have written the harmony into the text. Either way, the companions did not see Jesus, and Acts records no word from any of them.

Acts 9 has the companions standing: Paul "fell on the earth", while "the men who traveled with him stood speechless" (Acts 9:4, 7). In Acts 26 everyone falls: "When we had all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice" (Acts 26:14).[2]

Christian readers suggest that all fell at first and the companions then stood. Neither account tells it that way; the sequence is built by joining the two. A harmony can be possible and still be invented, and it should be called what it is. The three versions are set side by side at Damascus: the accounts compared.

In Acts 9, Jesus tells Paul only to "enter into the city, and you will be told what you must do" (Acts 9:6). The commission comes through Ananias, a disciple in Damascus, to whom the Lord says: "he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel" (Acts 9:15). In Acts 22, Ananias delivers it to Paul in person (Acts 22:14 to 15).[2]

In Acts 26, Ananias is gone. Jesus speaks the commission himself, on the road: "I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you a servant and a witness ... to the Gentiles, to whom I send you" (Acts 26:16 to 17).[2] The New American Bible explains that the words here "reflect the dialogues between Christ and Ananias (Acts 9:15) and between Ananias and Paul (Acts 22:14–15) in the two previous accounts."[1]

That is a fair account of what happened to the text. Words that a disciple spoke in Damascus are placed, in the third telling, in the mouth of Jesus on the road.

In Acts 9, Paul is blind for three days, neither eats nor drinks, and is healed and baptised by Ananias (Acts 9:8 to 18). Acts 22 keeps the blindness and the command to be baptised (Acts 22:11 to 16).[2]

Acts 26 has no blindness, no healing and no baptism. The New American Bible notes that "no mention is made of Paul's blindness in this account", and that the task he receives is "the removal of other people's spiritual blindness."[1] A speech can leave things out. The pattern is still plain: in each retelling the details move towards the authority of the speaker.

Paul's own account in Galatians is older than Acts and written in the first person. After the revelation, "I didn't immediately confer with flesh and blood, nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia. Then I returned to Damascus. Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter" (Galatians 1:16 to 18).[4]

Acts has no Arabia. Paul stays "several days with the disciples who were at Damascus", preaches in the synagogues, and goes up to Jerusalem, where Barnabas brings him to the apostles (Acts 9:19 to 27).[2] Paul's purpose in Galatians is to show that his gospel came from no man, and his own chronology keeps him away from the apostles for three years.

The bottom line

Acts tells Paul's conversion three times, and the accounts differ on whether the companions heard the voice, whether they stood or fell, who gave the commission, and whether Paul was blinded and baptised. Paul's own account in Galatians differs from all three on what came next. A Catholic Bible attributes the differences to Luke's different sources and shows how words given to Ananias passed into the mouth of Jesus.

The event on which Paul's authority rests has no witness but Paul. His companions heard something or nothing and saw no one. The Quran names the disciples of Jesus as the ones who answered his call, "We are Allah's helpers" (3:52), and Paul was not among them.[5] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. New American Bible, Revised Edition, notes on Acts 9:1–19, 26:16 and 26:18 (Washington, DC: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops).
  2. Acts 9:1 to 27; 22:6 to 16; 26:12 to 18 (World English Bible).
  3. Daniel B. Wallace, Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics (Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 1996), pp. 133 to 134, on akouō with the genitive and the accusative in Acts 9:7 and 22:9.
  4. Galatians 1:15 to 19 (World English Bible).
  5. Quran 3:52, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
